title: Mentors Help You Climb Higher and Faster
author: Parker Houston
summary: Houston builds a case for deliberate mentorship out of a single premise borrowed from John Maxwell, that people do what people see. If behavior is largely imitative, then the choice of whom you watch is one of the highest leverage decisions available, and leaving it to chance sets a low ceiling on what you can become. The argument runs through an extended account of learning traditional rock climbing from Tom, an older firefighter he found through an online ad for a climbing partner. The structure of trad climbing turns out to be an accidental model of good mentorship: Tom led first and Houston followed, removing and inspecting each piece of protective gear as he climbed, then led the next pitch while Tom came up behind and audited his placements with blunt verdicts. Houston credits that apprenticeship with letting him climb Half Dome and Mount Whitney and, more to the point, with keeping him from building bad habits in the first place. He then converts the story into eight practices, including humbling yourself enough to be taught, asking directly for coffee rather than for the title of mentor, matching on values, expecting flawed mentors, and keeping different mentors for different domains and seasons. He closes on parents as primary mentors, arguing that habits are contagious and that working on your own is the most reliable way to influence your children.
points: The whole argument rests on treating imitation as the dominant mechanism of behavior change, which makes selecting whom you follow a leadership act rather than a passive preference.

The trad climbing apprenticeship works as a model because the format forces mutual inspection: the follower studies every placement the leader made, then has his own placements audited on the next pitch.
Houston recommends asking for coffee and bringing questions rather than asking someone to be your mentor, on the theory that experienced people are already eager to pass on what they know.
He argues against holding out for the ideal mentor and in favor of taking what a flawed one does well, plus keeping separate mentors for business, spiritual life, and marriage.
The advice that growth is never to be outsourced to an employer leads him to endorse paying for a coach, and to name parents as their children's primary and unavoidable mentors.
quotes: The first law of leadership is that people do what people see.” –John Maxwell

Whether we meet with a mentor for coffee, read their latest book, follow them on social media, or listen to their podcast—we increase the odds that we will take on more of those thought patterns and behaviors. And these thoughts and behaviors will influence the course of our lives.

Then it was my turn to lead the next pitch (the next section of the climb). When I ascended a route, Tom would make suggestions for what I could do better. Then, he would climb up behind me while he evaluated how I had placed each piece of gear in the cracks and crevices of the rock.
Needless to say, my time with Tom was utterly invaluable to accelerate my learning curve, and to avoid developing bad habits.
If you weren’t blessed with great role models, and you aren’t exposed to better examples, it will put a very low ceiling on your potential—as a leader and as a human.
We often underestimate the drive that people have to pass on what they know. Leaders are often eager to share their knowledge with the next generation—it brings a deep sense of purpose.
In our culture of rampant individualism, we have lost the appreciation for the wisdom of those who have gone before us. It is a great tragedy to go through life without mentors.
If you have kids, you are the primary mentor. They watch everything you do. Keep in mind, “More is caught than taught.” This is a great challenge. Our habits matter because they are contagious.
